<p dir="auto">No this cannot be done via extension. Why have extra overhead? Makes no sense.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">It's not so much about overhead as it is the significant effort it would take to implement and maintain such a feature. Using an extension is better for several reasons:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>JavaScript is much easier to work with than C++</li>
<li>There is significantly more documentation on JavaScript and Chrome extensions than there is the code structure of Chromium (which is basically none).</li>
<li>The Chromium codebase continually changes and restructures, whereas JavaScript and Chrome extension APIs stay relatively the same.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">I know for a fact that some of these features can be done via an extension, but others will probably require modifications to Chromium.</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Frankly Chrome can even read your clipboard. It's called Clipboard Hijacking and its done through HTML5.</p>
<p dir="auto">Chrome = Privacy nightmare.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Well I guess that's another one we'll have to add to the list.</p>
<p dir="auto">Though if you're very concerned about your privacy, then you should follow <a class="user-mention notranslate" data-hovercard-type="user" data-hovercard-url="/users/9Morello/hovercard" data-octo-click="hovercard-link-click" data-octo-dimensions="link_type:self" href="https://github.com/9Morello">@9Morello</a> 's advice. <p dir="auto">Brave has some anti-fingerprinting measures built-in. I'm not sure how well they work, or how they're implemented. Anti-fingerprinting is very important given how aggressive trackers have gotten.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Yeah, it's always better to have some protection than none.</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">The problem with, e.g., uMatrix is I can't recommend it to a non-power user. Even my partner who is otherwise web savvy is just going to start turning it off a lot or going incognito. Users are a weak link in the chain of trust/defense.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">That's a good point. I've generally assumed that most people using this project are already power-users, but I'm realizing that this isn't such a good assumption. Plus, it's not safe to assume that all power-users know much about this subject.</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Does anyone know how hard this would be as an extension? I don't mind working on that.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">The code that modifies the page isn't too bad. I don't remember all of the details, but you'll need to use <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/defineProperty" rel="nofollow">Object.defineProperty</a> and other "low-level" JavaScript APIs to manipulate objects in ways that are not well known.</p>
<p dir="auto">Where the real work comes in is implementing this in an extension, and especially when designing a UI to configure the behavior. You'll run into limitations and hassles that slow you down. For example, when injecting a script into the real page's DOM (not the read-only one presented to the content script), there is the problem that if the page's JavaScript runs first, you may not be able to overwrite the properties in time. I haven't found a good solution to that when I was researching.</p>
<p dir="auto">I've been planning to implement this approach into Disable HTML5 Autoplay long before I've thought about this use-case, but I haven't gotten around to it.</p></div></div><div data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">Imo, a simple setup for people with no tech knowledge at all, and still decent privacy-wise, would be just uBlock Origin with more lists enabled than default (specially the multipurpose lists). Still, there aren't (or I'm not aware about) easy to use, working alternatives to FF extensions like Self-Destructing Cookies and Decentraleyes. There is Packet Guard to manage cookies, but its interface isn't as easy to use as SDC. In the topic of privacy+ease to use, there is really no super easy way to select which sites you want to save cookies from.</p>
<p dir="auto">To keep this about fingerprinting: uBlock Origin helps in stopping fingerprinting elements from running, but for this specific issue, unfortunately I can't see a middle ground between just using a good blocker like uBO and script blocking with uMatrix or NoScript.</p>
<p dir="auto">Does anyone knows how Privacy Badger works? This part from their site seems relevant:</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">At a more technical level, Privacy Badger keeps note of the "third party" domains that embed images, scripts and advertising in the pages you visit. If a third party server appears to be tracking you without permission, by using uniquely identifying cookies (and, as of version 1.0, local storage super cookies and <strong>canvas fingerprinting</strong> as well) to collect a record of the pages you visit across multiple sites, Privacy Badger will automatically disallow content from that third party tracker. In some cases a third-party domain provides some important aspect of a page's functionality, such as embedded maps, images, or stylesheets. In those cases Privacy Badger will allow connections to the third party but will screen out its tracking cookies and referrers.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">The WebExtensions version of Decentraleyes can't come soon enough.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 to act upon it.</p>
<p dir="auto">(Perspective follows)</p>
<hr>
<p dir="auto">The main communication channel for our projects are through issues on GitHub (and in ungoogled-chromium's case, also Gitter). Even if creating an issue or using Gitter didn't require any sort of account to use, you will never get a complete and accurate picture of what your userbase wants; you only hear from those that have decided to put in the effort to help the project by contacting the developer. This is why I take every issue and comment with deep consideration, because the volume of information flow is low to begin with.</p>
<p dir="auto">I never fully understood that until I read the response to my project on Reddit and Hacker News. Back then, ungoogled-chromium took more aggressive measures to deal with its main objectives, which included disabling features (e.g. WebRTC was a big one). The response on those sites clearly showed that disabling these features was a bad idea that broke many use cases. Unless a project's relatively popular, chances are that people would just move on without bothering to tell the developer about their dislike for some design decisions (it takes effort and can easily come off as rude).</p>
<p dir="auto">This is why I generally try to move significant changes to the Chromium experience behind flags. I assign a relatively high priority to user experience and needs, so I have to play it safe here.</p>
<p dir="auto">Obviously, your changes in Bromite are much more subtle and nuanced than disabling a large feature like WebRTC. But doing so may cause subtle breakages that will frustrate the user more than an obvious error. The less technically inclined user may not realize what's happening and think Bromite is broken without reporting the issue.</p>
<p dir="auto">Again, this is just my perspective on the matter based on my own experiences. I don't know your intentions or long-term plans.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 flex-wrap"><div class="ReactionPopoverAnchor__B84pko"><button <p dir="auto">Also, regarding breakage: it is enough to give a look to the UI tests and unit tests of Chromium to realise that basically nothing can be changed without breaking some.</p>
<p dir="auto">In Bromite I am enjoying this "freedom to break" as I experiment with things and make users participate to this experiment (with the pros/cons you described). I can do this now as there is a small user base, and I am aware that it might detract from it; in the past I did some "pre-releases", to get the user feedback. However the fact the users are few and not educated to report bugs doesn't allow me to do this proper.</p>
<p dir="auto">So, in short:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>user base grows -> more conservative development choices, possibility to have dedicated testing from users</li>
<li>user base is small -> not much testing aside from my own, since we are not updating or running the automated tests</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">I need more advanced users to follow the path you describe but I am just hanging around XDA and the user base (remember: Android) is not so advanced except for a few welcome exceptions.</p>
<p dir="auto">To go back on the topic of options to toggle features: the biggest problem on Android is the lack of extensions support; this seems on-topic: <a href="https://github.com/brave/browser-android-tabs/issues/316">https://github.com/brave/browser-android-tabs/issues/316</a></p>
<p dir="auto">So without any type of extension support available, the fallback is to implement patches/mini-features as I am doing, trying to limit the scope. I have seen how you implemented the Clear HTTP cache feature, however that is not available in the Android UI if I understood correctly the patch?<br>
For the features I am working on (not just fingerprinting mitigations) I plan to eventually add some Android-specific UI (since that is my main focus), I have not yet become "good enough" to tackle that. The codebase is huge, the recent addition of an official Chromium mirror to Github helps in this task.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sorry for the long post; I wanted to post here as a heads-up that something is being done on my side, but I know there are differences on approach/requirements.</p>
<p dir="auto">I have successfully implemented the getClientRects/getBoundingRects randomisation, patch to be published with next release of Bromite. <p dir="auto">There would need to be additional changes for it to work on Android, yes. The chain of functions to call should be similar, if not identical.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Yes. The part that I believe is more complicated is what you mention afterwards, having flags per-tab and per-site.</p>
<p dir="auto">You can see how easily I implemented a toggle for Javascript (<a class="issue-link js-issue-link" data-error-text="Failed to load title" data-id="296382772" data-permission-text="Title is private" data-url="https://github.com/bromite/bromite/issues/37" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/bromite/bromite/issues/37/hovercard" href="https://github.com/bromite/bromite/issues/37">bromite/bromite#37</a>) in next release of Bromite in this patch: <a href="https://github.com/bromite/bromite/blob/master/patches/BRM046_Add-menu-option-to-toggle-global-Javascript-preference.patch">https://github.com/bromite/bromite/blob/master/patches/BRM046_Add-menu-option-to-toggle-global-Javascript-preference.patch</a></p>
<p dir="auto">Before this implementation, I was going for the full-range approach e.g. having it implemented in the NavigationEntry (per-tab), including the session serialisation part. I gave up because I could not easily understand how the Javascript setting goes from Chromium preferences to the Webkit engine, but in general I believe it's doable to implement this and similar features per-tab/per-site.</p>
<p dir="auto">I believe Chromium should have these features upstream; see also: <a href="https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=826681" rel="nofollow">https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=826681</a> (@Primokorn reported that one for cookies). However I am not making any effort to upstream the changes...I kinda gave up on that.</p>
<p dir="auto">For the <code class="notranslate">getClientRects</code>,<code class="notranslate">getBoundingClientRect</code> fingerprinting mitigation I published the Bromite patch ahead of the
